newsitem.title: JAPAN: DKB not problem for all Japan banks - banking chief.
newsitem.headline: DKB not problem for all Japan banks - banking chief.

text.p: Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd's (DKB) alleged links with racketeers are only a problem for one individual bank, not for the Japanese banking industry as a whole, Naotaka Saeki, chairman of the Federation of Bankers Associations of Japan, told reporters on Tuesday.
"This is only a problem for one bank, I believe," Saeki said.

Asked about the banking industry's ties with corporate racketeers, he said, "There are some opinions that this is a problem in the whole banking industry, but I don't think other banks have such ties."
Saeki, who is also president of Sanwa Bank Ltd, said that his bank has not had any ties with racketeers since racketeer pay-offs were banned by a revision of the Commercial Code in the early 1980s.
He said that the federation will keep a close watch over developments in the investigation of DKB by prosecutors and the Finance Ministry.
He added that the federation might take action against DKB, although he did not specify what measures were under consideration.
He said that it would be regretable if, as a result of the DKB case, the Finance Ministry decides to change the banking act to impose stricter penalties on banks which violate the act.

Top executives at DKB, a major Japanese commercial bank, resigned last Friday and the bank admitted that it had been unable to cut its ties with racketeers now under arrest on suspicion of taking illegal payoffs from Nomura Securities Co Ltd.
Some domestic media have seized on the scandal as proof of deep-rooted ties between Japan's financial sector and the underworld.
A senior Finance Ministry official told Reuters on Monday that the ministry is now considering whether DKB's activities violated banking laws and, if so, what steps will be taken.
The ministry's decision regarding DKB, however, will depend on progress in prosecutors' investigation of the racketeer payoff scandal at Nomura, the official said.
He added that the ministry had begun to consider whether it should seek stricter penalties under the banking act for banks that deceive ministry inspectors.

DKB executives told reporters last Friday that the bank might have hidden from ministry inspectors dubious loans to a group linked to a racketeer, and that there might have been other similar misdeeds.
